title: GEMDAS
subtitle: The order the operations have to happen in.
objectives: Explain why an agreed order is necessary
Evaluate an expression in the correct order
Spot where a wrong order changes the answer

cards.title: Two people, one expression, two answers
cards.text: 4 + 3 × 2 is either 14 or 10 depending on what you do first. Maths cannot have that, so there is a rule.

cards.title: GEMDAS, in order of who goes first
cards.text: Work down the list. Within a level, go left to right.
points: **G**rouping. Brackets first, always.
**E**xponents next.
**M**ultiply and **D**ivide. Left to right, equal rank.
**A**dd and **S**ubtract. Left to right, equal rank.

cards.title: Which part of the expression goes first
cards.text: Choose which part to work out. A wrong choice shows you what it would give and why the rule says otherwise.

question.text: In 4 + 3 × 2, what do you do first?

cards.title: Multiply and divide do not outrank each other
cards.text: This is where most people slip. M does not beat D; they share a level.
points: **Left to right** when they share a rank.
**Add and subtract** work the same way.
**The letters are a list of levels**, not a queue of six.

question.explain: Equal rank, so left to right: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, then 4 × 2 = 8.

cards.title: Order matters when you put a fan back together
cards.text: You cannot fit the guard before the blade. Some sequences are fixed by the thing itself.
points: **Blade on the shaft**, then the front guard.
**Do it the other way** and nothing fits.
**GEMDAS is the same idea** applied to a calculation.
**The rule is not fussiness.** It is what makes the result repeatable.

cards.title: Brackets are how you overrule the order
cards.text: If you want the addition first, say so with brackets.
points: **(4 + 3) × 2 = 14.** The brackets promote the addition.
**4 + 3 × 2 = 10.** No brackets, normal order.
**Same digits, different answer.**
**Use brackets when you mean it.** They are not decoration.

cards.title: The gates open in an order
cards.alt: A ball on a track facing four gates in a row, the first open and the three behind it closed
cards.text: The ball cannot reach the second gate first. Neither can you.

cards.title: Every formula you have met already obeys this
cards.text: Kinetic energy is written ½ × m × v². The order is not optional.
points: **Square the speed first.** The exponent outranks the multiplying.
**Then multiply** by the mass, then by a half.
**Multiply before squaring** and you get a completely different number.
**That is why** the square law hits so hard.

cards.title: Damage formulas run on this exact order
cards.text: Base damage, then a multiplier, then a flat bonus. The order decides whether a build works.
points: **(base + flat) × multiplier** is very different from **base + (flat × multiplier)**.
**Stacking order** is why two similar builds perform differently.
**Patch notes argue about brackets** more often than you would think.
**The game engine obeys GEMDAS.** It has no choice.

terms.def: Brackets and anything acting like them.
Operations on the same level, done left to right.
Work an expression down to a single number.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Grouping, exponents, multiply/divide, add/subtract.
Equal ranks go left to right, not letter order.
Brackets exist to overrule the default.
The rule exists so one expression has one answer.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 4 Math, GEMDAS, the middle of the scope's three exponent weeks. The order is introduced as a necessity rather than a convention to memorise: the opening card shows one expression producing two answers, and the rule is presented as the fix. The interactive is the centre of the lesson. He picks the first move and a wrong pick is answered with what it would give and which rule overrules it, so the error is worked through rather than marked. The equal-rank point gets its own card and checkpoint because M-before-D is the misconception the acronym itself causes.
discussion: Does M really come before D?
When would you add brackets on purpose?
extension: Put the same digits in a calculator with and without brackets.
Write an expression that equals 20 in two different ways.
misconceptions: That the acronym is a queue of six steps rather than four levels.
